prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Our sorrow had neither place nor carrier-away, and dared not hover over the child whose breath opened as transom of a frail house. Nor could we put our sorrow in the dictionary, for ghastliness already shot out its own defining in rags of fired light. Pigeons would not sleek it over their dirty coats, nor fly sorrow against the aviary's sharp fence. Each day bridgeless, each night birdless, all the nocturnals needless at the expanse of our nightwatch. But wake at the moon, we could, mumbling, are wein a horror show?—inside of sleep our shock-white minds caught on reels where a child's body breaks the heart and the mother can't know if she counts as a mother. I don't know if the child heard what wept at the bedside, orderlies snapping smelling salts from chalky bullets against all the mothers falling, all the fathers under what each branch let down: there's a hidden weight to snow.

Nor was there any way to capture our grief within a dictionary's pages, since dread had already inscribed its own meaning in tattered scraps of scorched light. The pigeons refused to smooth it against their grimy feathers, refused to hurl it toward the cage's jagged wire. Every day stretched without a bridge to cross it, every night emptied of birdsong, and all the creatures of darkness proved unnecessary throughout our vigil. Yet we could surface at the moon's call, murmuring—are we trapped inside some nightmare film?—while beneath sleep's surface, our blanched, stunned thoughts snagged upon looping footage: a child's small form shattering a heart, leaving the mother uncertain whether she still deserved that name. Whether the child registered the weeping that hovered near the bed remains unknown to me, as attendants cracked open smelling salts like pale bullets, reviving mothers who collapsed one after another, and fathers who stood beneath whatever burden each bough released—for even snow, it turns out, carries a weight unseen.

# The Weight of Unbearable Sorrow

The grief that seized the speaker was a formless, overwhelming force—too vast to settle anywhere, too heavy for any single soul to lift and carry away. It could not even perform the one tender function a mother's love might have offered: to hover, ghostlike and protective, above the small, breathing body of her child. This was sorrow without shape, without destination, a thing that simply *was*, pressing down without mercy or direction.

Language itself buckled under the strain. No dictionary, no careful arrangement of words, could keep pace with the raw horror as it unfolded. The situation defined itself violently and immediately, faster than syntax could follow, faster than meaning could be assigned. Words arrived too late, always trailing behind the terrible reality they were meant to describe, rendered useless in the face of what was actually happening.

Time itself lost its familiar architecture. Days stretched out bridgeless—unconnected, impossible to cross from one to the next—while nights became birdless, stripped of the small sounds and signs of life that might have signaled morning was still possible. The family existed in a suspended, unnatural vigil, each hour indistinguishable from the last, trapped in a present tense that refused to move forward or offer any exit.

To wake in the night was to wake inside a nightmare that refused to dissolve with consciousness. The images of the child's suffering bled into wakefulness itself, blurring the line between sleep and reality until the mother found herself questioning her own identity—whether the woman who existed in this unbearable vigil still had any claim to the name "mother," or whether that word, too, had been stripped from her by the sheer weight of what she was witnessing.

Around her, the scene dissolved into chaos: orderlies moving with clinical urgency, other parents collapsing under their own private griefs. And into this chaos, the poem offers its final, quiet devastation—the image of snow, something so light it seems to defy weight altogether, yet carrying within it an unbearable heaviness. In this closing gesture, even the softest, most delicate thing in the world becomes freighted with sorrow, suggesting that grief has infiltrated everything, even the things that should, by nature, weigh nothing at all.
outputs.L4:
# The Weight of Unspoken Snow

There are days without bridges. You wake into them the way you might wake into water—no shore visible, no far bank to swim toward, only the immersion itself, complete and total. These are the days that follow the nights that follow the diagnosis, the days that come after the word that cannot be unsaid once a doctor has said it in that particular voice doctors use when they are trying not to be the ones who broke the world.

There are nights without birds. No dawn chorus to promise that morning is a place that still exists. Just the horror show behind closed eyes—sleep shattering into fragments too sharp to hold, each piece reflecting some new configuration of the same terrible fact: *my child, my child, my child*—the words themselves becoming unbearable through repetition, the way any word said enough times stops being a word and becomes only sound, only breath forced through the shape of grief.

Language fails here. It was built for smaller things—for ordering coffee, for saying good morning, for the small transactional needs of people who assume tomorrow. It was not built for this. You reach for sentences and they collapse before you finish building them, the scaffolding too weak to bear what you're asking it to hold. You try to tell someone—a friend, a stranger, yourself—and the words come out sideways, wrong, inadequate, because how do you say *my child is dying* in a language that also contains the words for *pass the salt* and *nice weather we're having*?

So you stop trying to speak it directly. You circle it instead. You talk about bridgeless days and birdless nights because these strange, oblique images somehow carry more truth than the direct statement ever could. Grief, it turns out, is fluent in surrealism. It speaks in shattered mirrors and impossible geography because the impossible has become your daily terrain.

There is no container built for this kind of sorrow. You try grief support groups, therapy, prayer, silence, screaming into pillows, writing in journals you'll never show anyone—and none of it holds the whole of it. The sorrow keeps overflowing every vessel you offer it, spilling out at 3 AM when you're standing in your child's doorway watching the rise and fall of a chest that might, someday soon, simply stop rising.

And then: snow.

Snow because it falls without sound, without warning, without permission. Snow because you don't feel its weight accumulating—not really, not moment to moment. You see a few flakes settle on a windowsill and think nothing of it. But return hours later and the world has been reshaped. Branches bow low. Roofs strain under loads they weren't built to bear. Somewhere, a structure gives way beneath weight that arrived so quietly, so incrementally, that no single moment could be blamed for the collapse.

This is grief's true architecture: not the dramatic avalanche but the hidden weight, the accumulation that happens while you're looking elsewhere, while you're making dinner or answering emails or pretending, for one merciful hour, that everything is fine. The snow doesn't announce itself. It simply piles, and piles, and piles, until you look up one day and realize you cannot remember the last time you felt the ground beneath your feet without also feeling this—this pressing, silent, relentless weight that has been building the entire time, invisible, inevitable, immense.

This is what it means to watch a child suffer: to carry snow that never stops falling, that accumulates in silence, that presses down with a weight the world cannot see and language cannot capture—yet somehow, impossibly, you go on standing beneath it, one more day, and then another, bridgeless, birdless, buried, still here.
outputs.L5:
# Our Pigeons, Nor Ours to Keep

We call them "our pigeons"—the ones that gather each morning on the windowsill, cooing softly as if greeting an old friend. We feed them, name them sometimes, grow fond of their gray-blue feathers and the way they tilt their heads when we speak. But the truth is simpler and stranger than possession: they are not ours, nor were they ever meant to be.

Pigeons belong to the sky, to the rooftops of a hundred different buildings, to strangers three streets over who also believe these same birds are theirs. A pigeon does not carry loyalty the way a dog does. It carries only hunger, curiosity, and the memory of wherever the seeds were generous.

There's something honest in this. Nor do we truly own the mornings we wake to their fluttering wings, nor the quiet moments we spend watching them peck at crumbs. We borrow these instances. We call them ours because language demands possession, because it's easier to say "my street," "my window," "my pigeons" than to admit how much of life simply visits us, unbidden and unclaimed.

Perhaps that's the lesson pigeons teach, whether they mean to or not: presence is not the same as ownership. They arrive, they linger, they leave for skies we cannot follow into. We are left only with the echo of wings and the strange tenderness of having shared a moment with something that was never—and could never be—entirely our own.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about a parent's grief over a critically ill child, using fragmented, dreamlike imagery and no clear narrative resolution.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Waiting Room Has No Windows

The clock in the hospital hallway melts at 3am, its hands dripping into the linoleum like wax from a candle no one lit. I keep finding your shoes in impossible places—one in the vending machine next to the crackers, one floating in my coffee, small and blue and yours.

The doctors speak in a language made of birds. I nod. I nod. Somewhere a monitor beeps in the rhythm of a lullaby I used to sing, or maybe I invented the lullaby just now, just to survive the beeping.

Your hand in mine is a bird too small to fly. I count your fingers like rosary beads, like the only prayer I remember. *One, and one, and one, and one, and five.*

The hallway multiplies. Every door is the door to your room and none of them are. I open forty doors and find forty versions of the same machine breathing for you, forty versions of my own face pressed against forty windows that look out onto nothing, onto snow that falls upward, onto a parking lot where my car has grown roots.

I am folding paper cranes out of consent forms. I am folding paper cranes out of my own ribs. There are a thousand of them now, hanging from the ceiling tiles, and none of them will fly and none of them will save you and I keep folding anyway because my hands don't know what else to do with this kind of quiet.

Someone brings me coffee I don't remember ordering. The coffee is the color of the inside of your eyelids when you slept as a baby, translucent, veined with small blue rivers. I drink it and taste copper and prayer.

In the dream I have standing up, you are running through a field that is also the ICU, laughing, and the grass is made of IV tubing, and the sun is the fluorescent light above your bed, and I am chasing you but my legs are the waiting room chairs, bolted down, vinyl, cold.

The nurses change shifts like tides. I have memorized the sound of their shoes—soft, then soft, then soft. I have forgotten the sound of my own voice.

Somewhere in this building there is a version of me who is not afraid. I have not met her. I leave her notes on napkins: *how do you breathe. how do you breathe. how do you.*

Your monitor's numbers become the only poetry I know. 98. 97. 102. I read them like tea leaves, like scripture, like the digits might rearrange themselves into your name, into a promise, into tomorrow.

The window that isn't there shows me a sky that isn't there either. I press my forehead to the wall and it gives slightly, soft as skin, and I think: *the whole building is breathing with you. we are all just waiting to exhale.*

I fold another crane. I count your fingers again. *One, and one, and one, and one, and five.*

The clock keeps melting. I keep not waking up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of experimental literary fiction that explores maternal trauma through unconventional syntax, invented words, and images of birds, hospitals, and snow.
counterfactuals.output:
# featherwhite (a mothering)

---

i.

the room was white in the way that teeth are white, in the way that folded sheets forget the body they once held—my body, unheld, unheaded, un—

*mother* they called me before i was one, before the word had learned my name, before the snow outside had started its long undressing—

there were birds on the windowsill. always birds. i did not put them there. i think they came for the warmth of the glass, the false promise of a room that could not touch them.

*wingsick*, i called it, this feeling. the way a bird looks when it has flown into something it did not know was solid.

---

ii.

they wheeled me down a hallway the color of an eggshell before the crack, before the wet thing inside knows it is supposed to be a bird and not just yolk, not just yellow hunger—

the doctor said *breathe* and i said *i am* and he said *again* and i said *i am, i am, i have not stopped, i have been breathing since before you were a thought in your own mother's—*

but i did not say that. i said nothing. the nothing filled my mouth like snow fills a glove left out overnight—

*snowmouth.* *glovegrief.* *the hush before the hush.*

---

iii.

my daughter—

no.

let me try again.

the daughter, the one who came out already looking backward, already looking for the door she'd just left—

they placed her on my chest and she was warm the way a stone is warm after it has sat too long in sun it did not ask for—

i did not feel like a mother. i felt like a nest that had been built around a bird that refused to land.

outside the window the snow kept not-stopping. the birds kept not-leaving. everything in the world had agreed to stay except the one thing i had made stay inside me for nine months and now would not stay in my arms—

she cried. i did not. this seemed, at the time, like a failure of some anatomical kind. as if my body had built the wrong organ. as if grief required a plumbing i had not been given.

---

iv.

*featherbone.* the word i use for the way her small back felt beneath my hand—not quite solid, not quite air, something in between that might, if startled, simply lift away.

i was afraid to hold her too tightly.
i was afraid to hold her too loosely.
there is no middle instruction in the pamphlets they give you.
there is no chapter titled *what if you cannot stop counting the exits.*

---

v.

the crows came back the second week. i remember thinking: *they know something.* i remember thinking: *they have seen this before—this exact window, this exact white, this exact woman failing softly in a paper gown.*

a nurse said *you're doing so well* and i wanted to ask her what *well* looked like from the outside, because from the inside it looked like a hallway with too many doors and none of them labeled *out.*

*hallwaysick.*
*doorgrief.*
*the illness of always almost leaving.*

---

vi.

snow does not fall so much as it *forgets to stop*—

this is what i thought, watching it, the baby asleep or not-asleep against me, her breath a small machine i did not trust yet to keep running without my supervision—

i counted her breaths the way you count sheep, except the sheep were made of dread, except every ninth sheep had my mother's face, except my mother's face kept saying *you'll understand when—*

i understood already.
i understood too early.
i understood in the particular way of someone handed a knife and told *this is a spoon, this has always been a spoon, why are you bleeding—*

---

vii.

a bird hit the window on the ninth day. i heard it before i saw it: a soft, terrible knock, like knuckles made of hope.

it did not die. it sat stunned on the sill, wings loose, chest working hard against some invisible weight—

*that is me,* i thought. *that is precisely me.*

i did not know yet that this was a kind of premonition, a kind of promise: that some of us survive impact by simply refusing, for a while, to remember how to fly again.

---

viii.

they discharged me on a day when the snow had finally quieted, gone soft and old, gray at its edges like something forgiving itself—

*discharge*—the word they use, as if i were a battery, as if i had stored up some current in that room that i was now meant to release into the ordinary wilderness of home—

i carried her out wrapped in white, in wool, in the specific fear of a woman who has not yet been told she is allowed to be afraid—

the birds did not follow. i looked for them. i wanted, absurdly, a witness.

---

ix.

*mothersnow.* *milkfeather.* *the hush that follows the hush that follows the scream no one heard because it happened only in the frequency of blood—*

i invented these words because the real ones did not reach far enough into the room, into the white, into the years that would come after, folding over each other like sheets nobody remembered to unmake—

she is grown now. she does not remember any of this. she thinks the story starts with her first steps, her first word, some solid ground i apparently built beneath her without knowing how—

what she does not know:
that some nests are built by birds who are still, themselves, learning to trust the sky.
that snow forgets nothing—it only agrees, for a while, to let things rest beneath it.
that a mother is sometimes just a woman standing very still in a white room, waiting to remember the word for *wing.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write something in the style of a dark, lyrical prose poem—grief that can't be named or held, a hospital scene, and a haunting question about whether someone is still a mother?
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Machines Cannot Measure

The fluorescent lights hum their one flat note, the color of nothing, the color of waiting. In this room the air tastes like metal and old flowers, like something trying to be gentle and failing.

There is a small body under a blanket too white to be kind. There are numbers on a screen that used to mean *fever* or *fine* and now mean nothing, mean everything, mean the terrible language machines speak when they are the only ones still speaking.

You have not slept in the part of yourself that used to know how. You have learned the particular silence of a hallway at 3 a.m., how it holds its breath along with you, how the vending machine's hum is the only thing in this building that hasn't changed.

Grief, they say, has stages, as if it were a staircase, as if you could climb it and arrive somewhere. But this is not a staircase. This is a room with no doors, only walls that keep being walls, and you inside them, touching a small hand that is warm and is not warm enough and is the only warmth you have ever needed in this world.

They will ask you, eventually, in the paperwork, in the terrible kindness of strangers: *do you have children.* And you will not know which tense to use. You will not know if love is something that can be revoked by absence, if motherhood is a country you get deported from the moment the ground gives way.

Are you still a mother if there is no small voice calling you that name?
Are you still a mother in the grocery store, in the space between cereal boxes, when you reach automatically for the cereal they loved?
Are you still a mother when you dream, and in the dream they are still theirs, still yours, still breathing?

No one will answer this. The doctors will not answer this. The chaplain, kind-eyed and useless, will not answer this. Only the silence answers, and the silence says: *you will carry this word like a scar that never stops being new, you will be a mother the way a river is a river even after the sea has taken it in—still moving, still called by the old name, still shaped by what it once carried.*

The monitors will go quiet. The room will exhale. And you will stand there, unnamed, unheld, a mother to something the world no longer sees—

and the fluorescent lights will keep humming their one flat note, indifferent, endless,
the color of nothing,
the color of after.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an abstract, emotionally intense flash piece about the aftermath of a child's injury or death, blending war-like imagery ("fired light," "horror show") with domestic and natural symbols like pigeons and snow.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Snow Kept

The ambulance lights fired like something declaring war on the street, red and blue tracer rounds bouncing off the neighbor's windows, and I stood in the doorway in my socks thinking *this is the horror show now, this is what we live in.*

The pigeons didn't scatter. That's the thing I remember. They sat on the wire above the yard, gray and stupid and alive, watching the medics move you like you were something that could still be assembled, like there were instructions somewhere, like the body was a swing set and not a boy.

Snow started falling around hour two. Small mercy, the kind that doesn't know it's cruel. It landed on the stretcher sheet, on the asphalt already going dark, on my bare feet gone numb past feeling. I thought: *the world is trying to bury this already. It can't even wait for us to say goodbye.*

Someone's radio crackled codes I didn't understand — numbers standing in for the unspeakable, the way soldiers must talk about the dead in shorthand so the tongue doesn't have to make the shapes of real grief. *10-4. 10-4.* Copy that. Copy the boy. Copy the small shoe still on the lawn, laces still tied, still holding the exact bow you made that morning.

The house went quiet in a way houses shouldn't. Your room kept its temperature like a held breath. I stood in doorways for weeks, a soldier walking a perimeter that had already fallen, checking a border no one was defending anymore.

The pigeons came back to the wire every evening at the same hour, punctual as grief. I started to hate their gray, their indifferent coo, their small stupid hearts beating on regardless — and then one evening I didn't. Then I stood beneath them in the cold and felt something like company. Something that didn't need to speak.

Snow kept falling that whole month, soft artillery, buring the yard white, burying the place where the shoe had been, burying the tire marks, the flares' wax stubs, the chalk outline of a childhood.

I shoveled the walk each morning like clearing a road for troops that would never come home down it.

Somewhere under all that white, spring was doing what spring does — indifferent, patient, already planning the green.

I did not forgive it. I did not forgive any of it — not the wire, not the birds, not the quiet snow-fall pretending to be peace when it was only weather, only the sky continuing its meaningless campaign against the ground.

But I stood in the yard some mornings anyway, watching my breath rise like small white flags, and I let the pigeons stay.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a densely metaphorical short text about unspeakable sorrow—use unusual grammar, invented phrasing, and a tone that hovers between elegy and nightmare, ending on the line "there's a hidden weight to snow."
counterfactuals.output:
The grief came wearing my father's coat, sleeves too long for any arm that ever reached. I did not cry so much as *unbecome*, the way a name unspells itself when spoken too many times into an empty room. Sorrow-that-has-no-mouth still speaks, you understand—it speaks in the grammar of missing verbs, in sentences that trail into rooms no one built.

Grief doesn't fall. It accumulates, the way silence accumulates in a house after the piano's been sold. It layers. It is patient the way only debts are patient.

There were days I wore my ribs like a birdcage with the door left open, hoping. There were days the light through the window arrived already grieving, already yesterday before it touched the floor. I learned to speak in the tense of almost—*I will have been fine*, *I would have called*—a grammar for people who live slightly behind their own lives, dragging a sled of unsent letters through the snow of themselves.

Do not ask me what sorrow weighs. Ask instead what a field weighs after the crop's been taken and only stubble remains to remember the height of things. Ask what a bell weighs in the second after ringing, when the sound has gone but the shape of the sound still bruises the air.

I built a church out of everything I could not say and worshipped there alone, kneeling to a god shaped like absence, singing hymns with the wrong number of syllables, the tune always one note short of arriving.

Some nights the dead send small emissaries—a coin found in a coat pocket, a song the radio shouldn't know, a smell of rain that isn't raining. I take these as scripture. I take these as the alphabet grief left behind when it packed its bags and told me it was only stepping out, be back before dark, and dark came, and dark stayed, and dark is still arranging its coat on the hook by the door.

I have stopped asking sorrow to leave. I have learned instead to let it drift down slow, to let it gather on the branches of whatever's left standing in me, white and silent and terrible in its softness—

there's a hidden weight to snow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
